blocks.p: You know the Polyvagal Theory. Now what? How do you apply this knowledge to your specific, everyday life? This is the third of five tips that answer that one question. It focuses on bringing a smidgen of compassion to your stuck defensive polyvagal state through two skills: validating and normalizing. Don't let this scare you. I promise I'll make it easy, and I'll walk you through it.

Ideally, we have lots of access to the ventral vagal safety state. Realistically, we don't. This is true for all of us, but more so if you've lived through a traumatic incident, or a life full of traumatic incidents, plus whatever social and family layers are stacked on top of those.

To put it simply, you could probably use a bit of compassion. Some understanding, some empathy, some validation, and to just feel normal. The problem is that neither you nor I can make that happen. We don't control other people. But I can teach you to provide it for yourself, in a few steps.

The goal here is to validate and to normalize your experience. We'll start with validating: what it is, why we'd do it, and then a really light, easy practice. Then we'll do the same with normalizing.

Validating means acknowledging what is true. We're more concerned with the internal world than anything else. So typically we validate, or acknowledge, what is true in our emotions and our thoughts. Those are usually more accessible than the underlying impulses and sensations that come from a polyvagal state.
Validating sounds like:
We can validate things that feel good and things that don't.

Validation is not being okay with, or liking, what you acknowledge. I'm not asking you to be okay with it. It's also not accepting it. You don't have to accept that it's permanent. You don't have to like it, and you don't have to accept it. We just have to recognize what is true.
Invalidation is judging yourself, saying things like, "There's something wrong with me," or "Other people aren't like this."

Invalidation also uses what I call cognitive skills. These are things we do to lessen the true nature of what we're going through, to reduce how overwhelming it is: minimizing, denying, repressing. It could sound like, "It's not a big deal," or "I just need to keep my mind off of it."

Invalidation also includes labeling or diagnosing your true experience. Saying "I feel distracted because of my ADHD" would be invalidating the true experience of distraction. It's enough to say, "I feel distracted," or "I am distracted," or "I feel overwhelmed," rather than "I feel overwhelmed because of X, Y, or Z."

I think we tend to overdiagnose, in the therapeutic world but also ourselves. I'm positive you may have tried to find a label for what you're feeling, and that you think of what you feel as a symptom of some sort of disorder, rather than the natural, expected consequence of the life you've lived. We'll come back to that in normalizing.
You might say, "I don't want to think about this stuff. I don't want to feel it. I don't want to talk about it. Justin, why the heck would I validate?"

Well, how can you get unstuck if you don't? If you don't acknowledge what's true, if you don't acknowledge how your stuck state shows up, how do you get unstuck? We have to be truthful. We have to acknowledge what is happening.

What would the alternative be? To continue to repress and minimize and ignore? Some sort of behavioral adaptation, like overeating, overexercising, overworking, or underworking? To keep your mind off it, to stay out of your body, to not feel it? Those coping skills and behavioral adaptations have served a purpose and gotten you this far. Okay. But they may not be working anymore, or they may not be postponing the issue like they used to. So it's time for something different. That's why we validate.

Have these other things made your life better? I doubt it. They may have gotten you here, but that's different from living a fulfilling life, different from finding actual happiness. That's just keeping your mind off stuff. It has a role, but I think that role may be played out at this point.

You validate by acknowledging what is true. Honesty is a huge part of validation. Your feelings are there, so be honest about that. You're not making this up. It's not random. You do have some level of stuck defense. We can start with those pieces. That's honest.

You also validate by connecting with the present moment and whatever it brings. You connect with the present moment through grounding and safety, using your senses, and then looking inward. You validate by noticing what you have inside of you, being honest about it, and naming it.

The good news is that you've already validated. You're here, reading this. Something is uncomfortable enough for you to be honest about it and then do something about it. So you didn't just validate, you're actually doing something about it as well. Congratulations.
Reflect on these questions:

ol: Could you validate somebody else's emotions? Could you acknowledge and name them? I bet you could.
Could a therapist or other helper validate your emotions? Could they acknowledge and name what you're going through? I would hope they could.

Can you validate yourself? This might be more difficult. Your answer might be, "I don't know how to, but I want to." We'll take care of that next. Or your answer might be, "No, I can't, I don't want to, and I won't." In that case, everything beyond this may not be helpful for you.

blocks.p: Before we try validating, how do you feel about validating? What comes up inside of you? What emotions come up? What thoughts pop into your brain? How do you feel about validating true experiences that maybe you've been minimizing or repressing? If you can name that, if you can say, "I feel anxiety about it," or "I feel fear," or "I feel overwhelmed," congratulations, you have validated yourself.
Now validate one experience of your stuck defensive state, or just whatever you're experiencing right now. That's fine too.
Say you're in a stuck fight state and you feel anger all the time. You'd validate it by saying, "I feel anger." "I do feel anger."
So just fill in the blank: "I do feel _." If you have a stuck shutdown state, you could probably validate experiences like hopeless or unmotivated. Fill in the blank again:

ul: "I don't like it, but I feel _."
"I hate to admit it, but yeah, I feel _."
"Fine, Justin. I guess I do feel _."

blocks.p: How did that feel, to acknowledge and name one emotion or one thing you're going through? Maybe it was uncomfortable, or anxiety producing, or maybe another emotion surfaced. If you can name how it felt to validate yourself, congratulations, you have validated yourself yet again. You're on a roll.
Now normalizing: what it is, why we'd do it, and then a practice, just like with validation.

Like validation, normalization is not being okay with or liking your valid experience. I'm not asking you to do that. It's not accepting that your experience is permanent either. You don't have to like it, and you don't have to accept it. What we want to do is validate it, and then normalize it. Normalization is also not judging yourself. It's not using those cognitive skills, and it's not labeling or diagnosing your valid experience.
So what is it? Normalization means making sense of your valid experience based on context. That context is past and present context, because the future isn't here yet.
Here's a weird question. Just roll with whatever pops into your mind: Is the number five normal? Does the number five make sense?

If you're confused, that's fine. If you have an answer, that's fine too. Let's build on it. Is five a normal result of two plus three? I would hope you say yes. Does five make sense within the context of four plus one? Again, I would hope you say yes.

So let's follow this logic. Is your stuck state normal, or expected, as a result of your life context? Does your stuck state make sense within the context of your relationships, your attachment, your professional life, and on and on? When you take these different pieces of context into account, does your stuck state make sense based on present and past context?

I believe your stuck state makes sense. In all my work, therapy and coaching, couples therapy, groups, psychoeducation, the community I run, it always seems to make sense. It doesn't seem random to me. I believe your emotional and cognitive experiences are there for a reason. They're the response to some sort of danger in your environment, past or present. Maybe not literal danger, like being attacked, but the way you were raised: the lack of healthy attachment, the lack of love, the lack of healthy communication, or maybe outright danger in your home. You neurocepted danger, and maybe you got stuck there.

That's an expected outcome of certain types of homes, relationships, or lifestyles. It makes sense why somebody would be stuck in defense based on that context. And if somebody else had your life, your context, they would likely have a similar stuck state.
Irene Lyon said it plainly when she was on the podcast:

q: It isn't your fault. It's not a genetic defect. It is a long-standing environmental situation brought on by crappy circumstances that were never addressed.

blocks.p: Normalizing is different from evaluating. Evaluating is rating it, saying it's good or bad. Normalizing is recognizing that a stuck state, whether shutdown, flight, fight, or freeze, is biological. It's not good or bad. It's not positive or negative. It just is.

It's an autonomic shift based on the context of your life, and maybe something you needed to exist in to get your needs met. And you are, at least in part, biological. I don't know what you believe as far as spirituality goes, but we're at least in part biological, right? So that biological shift from the past comes into the present, and is probably reinforced in the present.

So there's no value attached to this. It's not good or bad. It's not a reflection of your worth, and it's not a never-ending limit to your potential. It probably limits your potential now, but in the future, we don't know that.
Normalizing sounds like: "I am temporarily stuck in shutdown due to the context of my life."
Evaluating sounds like: "I'm in shutdown because something's wrong with me. Other people don't feel this way, even though their lives are worse than mine. I will never get better."
There's a clear difference in the way those two sound. Normalizing sounds like:

ul: "My feelings make sense in this context."
"Other people would probably feel similar. I see other people's feelings, and they make sense in their context. Mine are probably the same."

blocks.p: Reflect on these questions:

ol: Could you normalize someone else's emotions? Could you make sense of them? Say a friend tells you how sad they feel and how much grief they're going through. You'd probably say, "Yeah, you just lost someone close to you. That makes sense."
Could a therapist or other helper normalize your emotions and experiences? I would really hope so.
Can you normalize yourself? You might say, "I want to, but I don't know how." Okay. We'll take care of that next.

blocks.p: Before we get there, how do you feel about normalizing your experiences? What emotions, what thoughts, come up for you? What pops into your brain or your body as you consider it?
Now briefly normalize one experience of your stuck state, or whatever you're experiencing right now.

If something comes up within you that's a bit too much, use your sense of touch to release it. I think it's really helpful to squeeze, pull, or push, maybe into your palms. If you just need to get up and move around, go ahead and do that too.

ol: Validate it. "I do feel _." It can be the same thing as before or something brand new. Say you feel hopeless.

Lightly reflect on past context. Ever so lightly, reflect on past context that could contribute to your stuckness. If you feel hopeless, you might say, "In my past I've been let down a lot," or "I've never lived up to what I wanted for myself," or "People didn't believe in me," or "I was constantly rejected as a kid." Keep it pretty darn light. Just one sentence like that.

Lightly reflect on current context. Same thing, now with current context that could contribute to your stuckness. That could be behavioral or cognitive adaptations, things you do to feel better that don't really help: "I tend to overeat," or "I isolate myself a lot in darkness." Or maybe there's a relationship you're in, a friendship or a professional relationship, that is really keeping you stuck. Someone is invalidating your experiences, or putting lots of pressure on you to change. Those things can reinforce your stuckness. Again, keep it really, really light.
Normalize it. When you take those contexts into account, does it make sense why you're stuck, and why you stay stuck? Does it make sense why you think and feel the way you do?

blocks.p: If I felt hopeless, and I was raised in a home where I didn't really have healthy attachments with my caregivers or receive positive encouragement, and now I'm in a relationship where this person is pressuring me to be someone I'm not, would it make sense why I feel hopeless? Yeah, of course it does.
Take it a step further and create a short normalizing statement for your experience. Just fill in the blank:

ul: "I feel _, which makes sense based on the context of my life."
"I think _, which makes sense based on my life context."
"I always feel _, and I think anyone else would too."
"In the context of my life, my feelings of _ make complete sense."

blocks.p: Polyvagal ladder climbing is difficult. Self-regulation is difficult. Change is not easy, and not just for you. It's not a you issue. It's all of us.

All of this might be new, by the way. Change is difficult for anybody, but this inward, mindful, polyvagal self-regulation stuff might be brand new to you, and you've been however you've been for years, maybe decades. And here you are trying to change it. So let's normalize that. It's not easy. Change might not come easily, and that is very normal and very okay. And when you do change, it probably won't be all at once. It's going to be in slow, small steps.

Your stuckness is normal, but so are moments of connection. Even though you might be stuck in a defensive state, you have it within you to have at least small moments of connection. Here you are looking inward, learning, and trying to get more in touch with yourself. So moments of connection are possible. You're doing it right now. Even though you're stuck, there is some hope here. There are potentials for connection, not just with yourself, but with the outside world through your senses, and maybe with others, including your pets.

You're here. You didn't have to be here. You made a choice to be here. You've made many choices along this pathway. Maybe you've been to therapy or retreats, or tried medications, or this or that. You've probably made a bunch of choices, and here you are. This is another one. You're already on the path of change, and you are moving forward.

I know you want more. All you're doing is taking that next step, and hopefully learning to validate and normalize is a nice, solid next step for you. You are less stuck now than you were in the past, and in the near future you'll be even less stuck. Keep going down the path. You're not done yet. I don't think anyone's ever quite done. Hopefully we're always walking down the path of self-development and unstucking. You haven't gotten exactly where you want to be yet, but you're firmly on the path, and I hope this skill helps you keep walking.

You can use this little validation and normalization practice at any time. There's always something to validate or normalize. Right now, you're having some sort of experience you could validate and normalize.

As you practice this, especially with your stuck defensive state, you may notice other experiences come into your system. As you validate and normalize one experience, something else pops up. So it never really stops. Validation and normalization just keep going, indefinitely, in the present moment.

So that's your homework: keep practicing validation and normalization. Come back to this not just when you need it, but before you need it. Practice the skill before you move further down your polyvagal ladder into more dysregulation. Practice it when you have a positive emotion, like calm, just as much as when you have a negative one, like anxiety. These aren't really positive or negative, but we tend to group them that way.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.
